Look around the room you are in right now.
Touch the desk in front of you,
feel the cool air filling your
lungs, or gaze at the glowing screen
in your hands.
Everything you see, touch,
and experience feels solidly real.
It feels like the entire story of reality.
But what if all of this is
merely a small fraction of what
actually exists?
Modern astrophysics tells us
something deeply unsettling.
Everything humanity has ever
studied, from the smallest atom
to the most colossal galaxy,
accounts for only about 5 percent
of the cosmos.
Let that number settle for a moment.
Five percent.
If you gathered every star you
have ever seen, every planet,
every speck of dust,
every living thing, and put it
all in one pile,
that pile would be only a small
part of the whole.
The rest of the universe is
something else entirely, and it
is something we cannot see.
Today, we are going to follow the
trail of clues that led astronomers
to this humbling conclusion.
We will meet two of the biggest
mysteries in all of science,
dark matter and dark energy.
And we will ask the question that
sits underneath them both:
if most of the universe is
invisible, how do we even know
it is there?
First, let us think carefully about
that 5 percent.
Every grain of sand on Earth,
every drop of ocean water,
and every breath you take is made
of normal atomic matter.
So is our Sun,
along with at least one hundred
billion stars in our galaxy alone.
Even the distant supermassive black
holes and glowing clouds of cosmic
dust belong to this small family.
We have spent thousands of years
studying this small family of
things, and we have learned an
astonishing amount about it.
Yet, when scientists calculate
the total mass and energy of the
cosmos, all ordinary matter adds
up to just under 5 percent.
The remaining 95 percent is,
so far, invisible, silent, and unexplained.
That sentence deserves a second reading.
Not mostly known, with a few gaps.
Invisible, silent, and unexplained.
How did we realize that most of
reality was missing?
The answer did not come from a
single dramatic moment.
It came from astronomers who looked
closely at something that seemed
ordinary: how spiral galaxies rotate.
A spiral galaxy is a great wheel
of stars, turning slowly around its center.
It was a good place to test
whether our understanding of gravity holds up.
According to the established laws
of physics, stars near the outer
rim of a galaxy should move much
slower than stars near the crowded center.
It works just like our solar system,
where distant planets drift lazily
while inner worlds race around the Sun.
The farther you are from the center
of the mass, the weaker the pull,
and the slower you need to move
to stay in orbit.
So scientists measured the actual
speed of the stars far from the center.
And they encountered a profound shock.
The outer stars were moving
astonishingly fast.
They did not drift lazily at all.
They raced around the galaxy at
speeds that the established laws
of physics said they should not have.
In fact, these stars were moving
so rapidly that the visible gravity
of the galaxy could not possibly hold them.
Think of a ball whirled on a string.
If you spin it too fast,
the string cannot hold,
and the ball flies away.
By all ordinary logic,
these swirling galaxies should
have torn themselves apart and
flung their stars into the dark
void long ago.
Yet, they remain beautifully intact.
Something is holding them together.
Scientists suspect that an immense,
invisible halo of mysterious mass
surrounds each galaxy, providing
the extra gravitational glue needed
to hold everything together.
Notice the careful words: scientists suspect.
This is a hypothesis built to
explain what we observe,
not a substance anyone has held
in their hands.
Because this substance emits no
light, absorbs no light,
and reflects no light,
we simply call it dark matter.
The word dark does not mean it
is a dark color,
like black paint.
It means it is invisible to every
kind of light, so we cannot see
it with any telescope.
We can only notice what it does.
What could dark matter actually be?
It accounts for roughly 27 percent
of the entire universe,
dwarfing everything we know by
more than five times.
For every bit of ordinary matter
that makes up stars and planets
and people, there is more than
five times as much of this
mysterious substance.
Evidence strongly suggests it is
not made of protons,
neutrons, or electrons.
Those are the ingredients of
everything we know.
If a cloud of dark matter passed
through your living room right
now, you would not see it,
hear it, or feel it touch your skin.
It interacts with our world almost
entirely through gravity.
That is the only handle we have on it.
Gravity.
Dark matter tugs on stars and
galaxies, and we notice the tugging.
Leading hypotheses suggest it may
consist of undiscovered subatomic
particles that barely interact
with normal matter at all,
but no one knows for sure.
Honest science says it plainly:
we know where it seems to be,
and we do not know what it is.
As if a missing 27 percent were
not baffling enough, the universe
had an even bigger surprise waiting for us.
For decades, scientists assumed
that gravity would gradually slow
down the expansion of the universe
that began with the Big Bang.
It seemed natural.
Throw a ball upward,
and gravity slows it down.
The pull of all the matter in
the universe should be slowing
the expansion in the same way.
But when researchers observed
distant exploding stars across
cosmic time, they discovered the
exact opposite.
The expansion of our universe is
not slowing down.
It is speeding up.
Something seems to be pushing space
itself apart, overcoming the mutual
gravitational pull of all the galaxies.
Imagine tossing a ball into the
air and watching it rise faster
and faster, instead of slowing
down and falling.
You would immediately suspect that
something unseen was pushing it.
That is the feeling astronomers
had when they looked at those
distant explosions.
To explain this relentless cosmic
acceleration, scientists introduced
the concept of dark energy.
Dark energy makes up roughly 68
percent of everything that exists.
It is the largest piece of the
cosmic pie, bigger than ordinary
matter and dark matter combined.
Unlike matter, which clumps together
into stars and planets,
dark energy appears to be smoothly
woven into the very structure of
empty space itself.
It does not gather in lumps.
It is spread evenly through the
space between the galaxies,
and through the space inside this room.
In the simplest model,
dark energy is a property of space itself.
As the universe expands and creates
more empty space, more of this
mysterious energy appears with
it, so the push never runs out.
Space is not merely a container.
It represents the dominant
ingredient of our universe,
yet its true nature remains one
of the deepest mysteries in all of science.
We can measure its effect.
We can say how much of it
there seems to be.
But what it actually is remains unknown.
Before we put it all together,
it helps to pause and ask what
kind of knowledge this is.
When we say dark matter,
we are not describing something
we have captured in a laboratory.
We are describing a gap.
On one side, we have careful
measurements of how galaxies spin
and how the universe expands.
On the other side,
we have the visible matter we can count.
The two do not agree,
and dark matter is the name given
to the difference.
That distinction matters.
A name is not an explanation.
Imagine a detective who finds
footprints in the snow but never
sees the person who made them.
The detective can say the walker
was heavy, or moving fast,
or heading north.
But the detective cannot say who it was.
Dark matter is like those footprints.
We read its effect on the stars,
and we reason about what could
have left such a mark.
The same honesty applies to dark energy.
The measurements say the expansion
is speeding up.
The name dark energy is a label
for whatever is responsible,
a description of how it behaves,
not an answer to what it is.
It is also worth noticing how
different these two mysteries feel.
Dark matter acts like a glue.
It gathers around galaxies,
it pulls inward, and it helps hold
spinning wheels of stars together.
Dark energy acts in the opposite way.
It does not gather anywhere.
It pushes outward across the whole
universe, and it grows more
important as space grows larger.
One holds things together.
The other pushes everything apart.
Now consider how modest the clues were.
A star turning a little too fast.
A distant explosion looking a little
too faint.
None of these observations was
dramatic to the naked eye.
They were numbers in a notebook,
and the numbers refused to agree
with expectations.
Yet when astronomers trusted the
numbers instead of the expectations,
an entire hidden universe came into view.
Here is another way to hold the
idea in your mind.
Picture the surface of the ocean
on a stormy night.
Waves rise, foam gleams white,
and the foam is all you can
see in the dark.
If you only studied the foam,
you might build a detailed theory of foam.
But the foam rides on water,
and the water is vastly larger
than the foam.
Our stars and galaxies are the bright foam.
The dark ocean beneath is where
most of the universe lives.
So what should we feel about all of this?
Perhaps not fear, and not confusion,
but a quiet kind of excitement.
A mystery of this size means there
is still something enormous left to discover.
We do not yet know whether the
answer will be a new particle,
a new idea, or something no one has imagined.
Put these pieces together,
and the complete picture of our
reality becomes astonishingly humbling.
Normal matter makes up roughly 5 percent.
Dark matter claims about 27 percent.
And dark energy commands an
overwhelming 68 percent.
Together, dark matter and dark
energy make up about 95 percent
of the total cosmic pie.
Imagine walking into an enormous
library containing millions of
books, only to realize that you
can read merely five pages in a
single volume, while the rest are
written in an invisible ink.
You would not say you understood the library.
You would say you had barely begun.
That is where we stand with the universe.
So, the honest summary is simple.
We know how much seems to be there.
We know where dark matter seems to gather.
We know that the expansion is speeding up.
And we do not know what either
of the dark components really is.
That is not a failure of science.
It is the place where science is
doing its most interesting work.
And yet, this is not a story of defeat.
Astronomers noticed that stars
at the edge of galaxies moved too fast.
They noticed that distant exploding
stars revealed a speeding expansion.
They followed small oddities in
the data, and those oddities pointed
to something enormous.
Science does not shrink from such surprises.
It follows them, and in doing so
it learns the size of its own ignorance.
So when you step outside tonight
and look up at the night sky,
take a quiet breath and look past
the glowing pinpricks of light.
The stars and galaxies are not
the main show.
They are merely tiny specks of
bright foam floating on top of
a vast, unseen ocean.
We are conscious creatures made
of a rare, luminous minority,
striving to decipher the dark sea
that cradles us.
Perhaps the most remarkable thing
about the universe is that a small,
bright minority of it has learned
to ask what the rest is.
